readings.title: Into My Own
readings.challenge: Follow a wish through its “should” and “would” clauses, and decide how seriously the speaker means it.
readings.focus: A young speaker imagines walking into the dark woods for good, and imagines the people who would come after him: a poem about leaving that is also about being missed.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” “Into My Own” stands first in the book. “As ’twere” means “as it were,” so to speak; a mask hides what is behind it; the “edge of doom” is the end of the world, or of time; withheld means held back; to steal away is to leave quietly; e’er means ever.

excerpt.locator: “Into My Own,” complete poem; opens “One of my wishes is that those dark trees, So old and firm they scarcely show the breeze,…”; closes “…would not find me changed from him they knew— Only more sure of all I thought was true.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker wish about the dark trees, and what would he do if the wish came true?
facilitatorNotes: He wishes they were not just a dark front, “the merest mask of gloom,” but went on for ever, so that one day he could slip into them and never come out. The wish is huge (“unto the edge of doom”), and the plan is quiet: to “steal away.”
evidence: the merest mask of gloom
Into their vastness I should steal away

questions.prompt: Lost walkers usually long to find open land or a road. Why is this speaker “Fearless of ever finding” them?
facilitatorNotes: He reverses the usual fear: open land and a highway would bring him back to ordinary life, where “the slow wheel pours the sand” of a dusty road. He wants a world without ends. Ask what he might be leaving; the poem never says, so readers may supply a reason or notice that it is missing.
evidence: Fearless of ever finding open land,
Or highway where the slow wheel pours the sand.

questions.prompt: Who does he imagine following him, and what does he hope they will feel?
facilitatorNotes: The people who “should miss me here” and want to know if he still loves them. A poem about going off alone turns out to want company after all, or at least to be missed. Readers may find this lonely, a little proud, or a test of other people’s love.
evidence: who should miss me here
And long to know if still I held them dear.

questions.prompt: The last two lines say that they “would not find me changed.” Is that a boast, a promise or a comfort? Does it fit a journey into the unknown?
facilitatorNotes: Travellers usually come back changed; he expects only to be “more sure of all I thought was true.” Some readers hear a young man’s confidence, which fits the book’s title; others hear stubbornness, or reassurance to the people left behind. Ask which reading the words “Only more sure” support best.
evidence: They would not find me changed from him they knew—
Only more sure of all I thought was true.

readings.title: Ghost House
readings.challenge: Work out where the speaker lives when his house has vanished, and who his silent neighbours are.
readings.focus: An abandoned farm going back to forest becomes a home for the imagination, shared with birds, bats and the forgotten dead.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” In Frost’s New England many hill farms were abandoned as families moved west or into the cities; trees filled the fields, and only stone walls, cellar holes and small family graveyards were left. A copse is a thicket of young trees; a whippoorwill is a night bird named for its call; “mute” means silent; to “mar” is to spoil or blur; a lass and a lad are a girl and a boy.
readings.contentNote: The speaker’s silent companions are the dead of the old farm, buried under worn gravestones.

excerpt.locator: “Ghost House,” complete poem; opens “I dwell in a lonely house I know That vanished many a summer ago, And left no trace but…”; closes “…ever sings, And yet, in view of how many things, As sweet companions as might be had.”.

questions.prompt: What is left of the house, and what is taking its place?
facilitatorNotes: Only the cellar walls and an open cellar where raspberries grow. The woods are coming back into the hay field, the orchard has become a thicket, and the path to the well has grown over. Nature is quietly taking the farm back.
evidence: And left no trace but the cellar walls,
The woods come back to the mowing field;

questions.prompt: “The footpath down to the well is healed.” Why “healed,” as if the path had been a wound?
facilitatorNotes: A path is worn by feet; with no one walking it, grass closes over it like skin over a cut. The word can suggest that the farm was a wound in the forest, now mending, or, more sadly, how quickly people’s traces disappear. Readers can choose and defend one.
evidence: The footpath down to the well is healed.

questions.prompt: Who are the “mute folk” who share the place with him? Find the clues.
facilitatorNotes: The stones under the low tree are gravestones whose names moss has blurred, so the folk are the farm’s dead, among them “two, close-keeping,” a young pair buried side by side. They are silent, “slow and sad,” and none of them sings. He does not know their names.
evidence: Those stones out under the low-limbed tree
Doubtless bear names that the mosses mar.

questions.prompt: How can he “dwell” in a house that vanished, and why does he call the dead “As sweet companions as might be had”?
facilitatorNotes: He lives there in imagination, or returns there so often in mind that it is his true home; his “strangely aching heart” suggests loneliness. Calling the dead sweet company “in view of how many things” hints that living company has disappointed him, or that quiet company asks nothing. Some readers find the poem eerie, others peaceful.
evidence: I dwell with a strangely aching heart
As sweet companions as might be had.

readings.title: Love and a Question
readings.challenge: Follow a story told in a ballad’s beat, and work out the question the bridegroom cannot answer.
readings.focus: A man on his wedding night must choose between kindness to a homeless stranger and the privacy of his new marriage, and the poem leaves the choice open.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” This poem is written like an old ballad, a story-song with a steady beat and rhyming lines. “Spoke the bridegroom fair” means spoke politely to him; “for all burden, care” means he carried nothing but his troubles; woodbine is a climbing vine; a dole is a small gift to the poor; to harbor is to give shelter; woe is sorrow; to mar is to spoil.

excerpt.locator: “Love and a Question,” complete poem; opens “A stranger came to the door at eve, And he spoke the bridegroom fair. He bore a…”; closes “…mar the love of two By harboring woe in the bridal house, The bridegroom wished he knew.”.

questions.prompt: What do we learn about the stranger, and how does he ask for shelter?
facilitatorNotes: He comes at evening with only a green-white stick and his “care,” and asks “with the eyes more than the lips,” then looks down a road with no lit window anywhere. He asks almost silently, perhaps from pride, perhaps from weariness, and there is nowhere else to go.
evidence: He asked with the eyes more than the lips
Without a window light.

questions.prompt: Instead of answering, the bridegroom says, “Let us look at the sky.” Why might he do that, and what do the signs of the weather say?
facilitatorNotes: He puts off answering by talking about the night ahead. Fallen leaves, blue berries and “winter was in the wind” all say it will be cold, so the weather argues for letting the stranger in. “Stranger, I wish I knew” sounds like a weather answer but hides the real question.
evidence: And question what of the night to be,
Autumn, yes, winter was in the wind;

questions.prompt: What is the bride doing, and how does the poem make her the reason the bridegroom hesitates?
facilitatorNotes: She bends over the fire alone, her face red with the coals and with “the thought of the heart’s desire.” He looks at the road but sees only her, and wants to lock her heart away “in a case of gold.” Readers may find that tender, or a little possessive.
evidence: Yet saw but her within,
And wished her heart in a case of gold

questions.prompt: The bridegroom would gladly give bread, money or a prayer. What does he not know? What would you do, and does the poem tell us what he did?
facilitatorNotes: Whether kindness requires him to “mar the love of two” by bringing sorrow into the house on its first night. The poem stops at “wished he knew,” so the title’s question stays open. Readers can argue for welcoming a traveller on a winter night, for a couple’s right to privacy, or that the stranger’s sorrow might not spoil anything at all.
evidence: The bridegroom thought it little to give
By harboring woe in the bridal house,

readings.title: Storm Fear
readings.challenge: Follow one long sentence through very short and very long lines, keeping track of who “we” are and what the wind “says.”
readings.focus: In a snowbound farmhouse at night, a father hears the storm as a beast calling him out, and admits a doubt that his small family can save itself.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” The whole poem is a single sentence. A chamber is a room; “stifled” means muffled; to “mark” is to notice; “subdued” means made quiet; a dooryard is the yard by a house door; the road is “ungraded” because drifts have made it rough and uneven; to “own” a doubt is to admit it.

excerpt.locator: “Storm Fear,” complete poem; opens “When the wind works against us in the dark, And pelts with snow The lower chamber window…”; closes “…my heart owns a doubt Whether 'tis in us to arise with day And save ourselves unaided.”.

questions.prompt: What does the wind do to the house, and what does it seem to say?
facilitatorNotes: It works “against us in the dark,” throws snow at the east window and whispers “with a sort of stifled bark,” like an animal at the glass calling “Come out! Come out!” Frost makes the storm a beast that dares the family to leave the house.
evidence: And whispers with a sort of stifled bark,
'Come out! Come out!—

questions.prompt: “It costs no inward struggle not to go, / Ah, no!” Is the speaker tempted? What might “Ah, no!” sound like?
facilitatorNotes: He is not tempted at all; nobody would go out into that. “Ah, no!” could be a shiver, a short grim laugh, or a man protesting a little too much. The real fear is coming, and it is not about going out.
evidence: It costs no inward struggle not to go,

questions.prompt: “I count our strength, / Two and a child.” Why does he count, and what are the others watching as the night goes on?
facilitatorNotes: He measures how few they are against the storm. The ones still awake watch the cold creep in as the fire dies and the drifts pile up, until “even the comforting barn grows far away.” The very short lines sound like counting.
evidence: Two and a child,
How the cold creeps as the fire dies at length,—

questions.prompt: What doubt does his heart “own” at the end? Why might “unaided” be the most frightening word in the poem?
facilitatorNotes: Whether they can get up in the morning and “save ourselves unaided,” digging out alone. On a lonely farm nobody will come, so the deepest fear is being on their own. Some readers take it as one bad winter night; others as any moment when a parent fears being unable to protect a family.
evidence: And my heart owns a doubt
And save ourselves unaided.

readings.title: Wind and Window Flower
readings.challenge: Follow a love story between two things that are not people, and decide whose side the poem is on.
readings.focus: A winter wind courts a house plant on a windowsill; she stays by the warm stove, and by morning he has blown far away.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” Window flowers are house plants kept on a sunny sill through the winter. “List” means listen; a pane is a sheet of window glass; the sash is the window frame; “perchance” means perhaps; to “prevail” is to win; “naught” means nothing.

excerpt.locator: “Wind and Window Flower,” complete poem; opens “Lovers, forget your love, And list to the love of these, She a window flower, And he a…”; closes “…aside And thought of naught to say, And morning found the breeze A hundred miles away.”.

questions.prompt: What does the first stanza ask lovers to do, and whose love story does the poem tell instead?
facilitatorNotes: To forget their own love and listen to the love of a window flower and a winter breeze. It opens like an old ballad that promises a love story, then gives the parts to a plant and the weather.
evidence: Lovers, forget your love,
She a window flower,

questions.prompt: What kind of suitor is the wind? Find what he usually cares about and what he does at night.
facilitatorNotes: He is “Concerned with ice and snow, / Dead weeds and unmated birds” and knows little of love. Yet he cannot help noticing her, comes back at dark, sighs on the sill and shakes the sash, which are the sounds people indoors hear on a windy night. Frost turns ordinary winter noises into courting.
evidence: Concerned with ice and snow,
He gave the sash a shake,

questions.prompt: What would the flower have to leave if she went with him? Why might she lean aside?
facilitatorNotes: The “firelit looking-glass / And warm stove-window light,” and her life, since a house plant cannot live in a winter wind. The caged yellow bird is another warm indoor creature. She says nothing, though he “half prevailed,” so she may have been tempted.
evidence: From the firelit looking-glass
But the flower leaned aside

questions.prompt: “And morning found the breeze / A hundred miles away.” How do you feel about the ending: sad, funny or wise?
facilitatorNotes: The wind does not wait or grieve; he simply moves on, as winds do. Some readers feel sorry for him, some think the flower chose wisely, and some hear a gentle joke about a wanderer courting someone who loves home. Point to the plain, quick last line.
evidence: A hundred miles away.

readings.title: Reluctance
readings.challenge: Follow a walk that ends, then a question that reaches far beyond the walk.
readings.focus: The end of a long walk and of autumn becomes a question about whether a heart should ever calmly accept an ending.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” “Reluctance” is the last poem in the book. To wend is to travel; “lo” is an old word for “look”; to ravel here is to loosen and let go; an aster is a late wild flower; witch-hazel (printed “wich-hazel”) is a shrub that blooms in late autumn; “whither” means where to; treason is betraying a loyalty.

excerpt.locator: “Reluctance,” complete poem (without the acknowledgment printed after it); opens “Out through the fields and the woods And over the walls I have wended; I have climbed the…”; closes “…To yield with a grace to reason, And bow and accept the end Of a love or a season?”.

questions.prompt: Where has the speaker been, and how does the first stanza end?
facilitatorNotes: Through fields and woods, over walls, up “the hills of view” to look at the world, then home by the highway, and “lo, it is ended.” A long journey is told in one breath and then simply stops; “lo” makes the ending sound announced.
evidence: I have climbed the hills of view
And lo, it is ended.

questions.prompt: Which leaves are not yet on the ground, and what do they do? Why might Frost single them out?
facilitatorNotes: The oak keeps some and lets them go “one by one,” scraping and creeping over the crusted snow “When others are sleeping.” The oak holds on, like the speaker who cannot let the season go. Readers may suggest other meanings: a last few things that refuse to end on time.
evidence: Save those that the oak is keeping
And let them go scraping and creeping

questions.prompt: “The heart is still aching to seek, / But the feet question ‘Whither?’” Explain the difference between the heart and the feet.
facilitatorNotes: The heart wants to keep going and searching; the feet, tired and practical, ask where there is left to go now the flowers are gone. Two parts of one person disagree.
evidence: The heart is still aching to seek,
But the feet question 'Whither?'

questions.prompt: The last stanza calls it “treason” to “yield with a grace to reason.” What is the speaker saying, and do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: Accepting the end “Of a love or a season” calmly and sensibly feels like betraying the thing you loved; the heart stays loyal to what is ending. Some readers agree that letting go too easily would be disloyal; others think graceful acceptance is wisdom. The title names the feeling rather than settling it.
evidence: To go with the drift of things,
Of a love or a season?

readings.title: My November Guest
readings.challenge: Work out who the guest is, and notice what the speaker knows but does not say.
readings.focus: The speaker’s Sorrow, pictured as a woman, loves the bare November days and thinks she is teaching him to see them; he has loved them for years, and lets her think so.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” In the book’s contents Frost gave each poem a one-line note; for this one he wrote, “He is in love with being misunderstood.” Fain means glad; to list is to listen; worsted is woollen cloth; sodden means soaked; to vex is to annoy; “it were vain” means it would be useless. In the 1915 printing “Sorrow” has a capital letter, like a name.

excerpt.locator: “My November Guest,” complete poem; opens “My Sorrow, when she's here with me, Thinks these dark days of autumn rain Are beautiful…”; closes “…coming of the snow, But it were vain to tell her so, And they are better for her praise.”.

questions.prompt: Who is the guest? How can you tell she is not an ordinary visitor?
facilitatorNotes: She is the speaker’s Sorrow, his sadness, imagined as a woman who comes to stay each November. The capital letter makes “Sorrow” a name, and she walks the lane, talks and wears a grey woollen dress like a real person.
evidence: My Sorrow, when she's here with me,
She's glad her simple worsted grey

questions.prompt: What does Sorrow love about autumn? Are these things most people would call beautiful?
facilitatorNotes: Dark rainy days, bare and withered trees, the soaked lane, the birds gone, mist on her dress, the faded earth and heavy sky. Most people find these gloomy; she finds them “beautiful as days can be.”
evidence: She loves the bare, the withered tree;
The desolate, deserted trees,

questions.prompt: Sorrow thinks the speaker has “no eye for these.” Is she right?
facilitatorNotes: No. He says he did not learn to love bare November days “yesterday”: he has loved them a long time. She scolds him for not seeing what he has seen all along.
evidence: She thinks I have no eye for these,
Not yesterday I learned to know

questions.prompt: Why doesn’t he tell her, and what does the last line mean?
facilitatorNotes: It would be “vain”: she would not believe him, or it would spoil her pleasure in showing him. And he likes hearing the days praised, which makes them “better.” Frost’s note says he is “in love with being misunderstood.” Some readers think he enjoys a little secret; others that he is being kind to his Sorrow, letting her feel she has something to teach.
evidence: But it were vain to tell her so,
And they are better for her praise.

readings.title: Stars
readings.challenge: Follow a sentence across three stanzas, and decide whether the stars are watching over us.
readings.focus: Countless stars seem to gaze down on people struggling through drifting snow, but the poem decides they see nothing at all.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” Frost’s note on this poem in the contents is “There is no oversight of human affairs”: no one is watching over what happens to people. To congregate is to gather in a crowd; tumultuous means wild and stormy; keenness is eager interest; faltering means stumbling; Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom, and old marble statues of her have blank white eyes with no pupils.

excerpt.locator: “Stars,” complete poem; opens “How countlessly they congregate O'er our tumultuous snow, Which flows in shapes as tall…”; closes “…stars like some snow-white Minerva's snow-white marble eyes Without the gift of sight.”.

questions.prompt: Where are the stars, and what is happening below them?
facilitatorNotes: Countless stars crowd the winter sky over snow that the wind heaps into drifts “as tall as trees.” The first stanza is a picture of a wild, bright, freezing night.
evidence: How countlessly they congregate
Which flows in shapes as tall as trees

questions.prompt: The stars seem to watch “As if with keenness for our fate.” What do they seem to be watching?
facilitatorNotes: People taking a few stumbling steps through the snow toward “white rest”: sleep, or perhaps freezing to death, and a resting place that will be covered and hidden by morning. Some readers see a traveller lost in a storm; others a picture of every life moving toward its end.
evidence: Our faltering few steps on
To white rest, and a place of rest

questions.prompt: “And yet”: how does the last stanza change the picture?
facilitatorNotes: The stars only seemed interested. They feel “neither love nor hate,” like the blank marble eyes of a statue of Minerva, goddess of wisdom, which cannot see. Even wisdom, in this picture, is blind to us.
evidence: And yet with neither love nor hate,
Without the gift of sight.

questions.prompt: Frost’s note says “There is no oversight of human affairs.” Is the poem frightening, comforting, or neither?
facilitatorNotes: It can feel lonely and cold: no one is watching over the stumbling walkers. But stars without hate do not judge either, and some readers find that calm. Others will disagree with the idea itself and say so; the poem is one person’s view on one cold night.
evidence: Those stars like some snow-white
Minerva's snow-white marble eyes

readings.title: The Vantage Point
readings.challenge: Follow the speaker’s eye from far to near, and think about what each view gives him.
readings.focus: Lying hidden on a hillside, a young man looks down on the far-off homes and graves of people, then rolls over and looks into an anthill.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” Frost’s note in the contents: “And again scornful, but there is no one hurt.” The poem is a sonnet, fourteen lines. A vantage point is a place with a good view. To hie is to hurry; cattle “keep the lawn” by grazing the grass short; lolling means lazily spreading; juniper is a low evergreen shrub; “whichever are to mind” means whichever I feel like thinking about; lo means look; a bluet is a tiny pale-blue wildflower; “bruisèd” is said in two syllables, as the accent shows.

excerpt.locator: “The Vantage Point,” complete poem; opens “If tired of trees I seek again mankind, Well I know where to hie me—in the dawn, To a…”; closes “…breeze, I smell the earth, I smell the bruisèd plant, I look into the crater of the ant.”.

questions.prompt: Where does he go when he is “tired of trees,” and what can he see from there?
facilitatorNotes: At dawn he goes to a hillside grazed by cattle and lies hidden among the junipers. Far off he sees the white houses of a town, and on another hill, farther still, its graveyard.
evidence: To a slope where the cattle keep the lawn.
Far off the homes of men, and farther still,

questions.prompt: “Living or dead, whichever are to mind.” How does he “seek again mankind”?
facilitatorNotes: From a distance, unseen, choosing whether to think about the living or the dead as he pleases. He wants people, but only at a safe distance and on his own terms. Frost’s note calls it “scornful,” though no one is hurt.
evidence: Myself unseen, I see in white defined
Living or dead, whichever are to mind.

questions.prompt: What happens when he turns over on his arm? Which senses take over?
facilitatorNotes: The view jumps from miles away to inches: the warm hillside on his face, his breath shaking a tiny flower like a breeze, the smell of earth and crushed plants. Seeing far gives way to feeling, smelling and seeing very close.
evidence: I have but to turn on my arm, and lo,
My breathing shakes the bluet like a breeze,

questions.prompt: Why end by looking “into the crater of the ant”? How is the anthill like the town?
facilitatorNotes: An anthill is a busy little town of its own, and he looks down on it as he looked down on the houses of men. “Crater” is a huge word for a tiny hole: to the ant he is a giant whose breath is a breeze. Readers may say the ending makes him humbler, or only shows that he prefers small creatures to people.
evidence: I look into the crater of the ant.
If tired of trees I seek again mankind,

readings.title: Spoils of the Dead
readings.challenge: Compare how the fairies meet death with how the speaker did, and decide what he is asking you.
readings.focus: Two fairies playing in the woods come upon a long-dead man and carry off his ring and chain as toys; the speaker remembers his own first meeting with death.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” Frost’s note in the contents is simply “about death.” Spoils are things taken from the defeated or the dead. To espy is to catch sight of; eerily means strangely, in a way that makes you shiver; nigh means nearly. The fairies are also called elves. In the book the “you” of the next-to-last stanza is printed in italics, for stress.
readings.contentNote: Two fairies find the remains of a man who died in the snow months before, and take his ring and chain to play with.

excerpt.locator: “Spoils of the Dead,” complete poem; opens “Two fairies it was On a still summer day Came forth in the woods With the flowers to play.”; closes “But I recognised death With sorrow and dread, And I hated and hate The spoils of the dead.”.

questions.prompt: How did the fairies come upon the man? What does “Flower-guided” mean?
facilitatorNotes: They were playing, picking flowers and dropping them for better ones further on, and the trail of flowers led them, running, to the body. Nobody meant to find it; play led them there.
evidence: The flowers they plucked
Flower-guided it was

questions.prompt: What clues tell you how long the man has lain there?
facilitatorNotes: The snow made his “feathery bed,” so he died in winter; the snow has been gone “A long time,” and his body is nearly gone too. He has lain alone in the woods for months.
evidence: The snow must have made
Nigh gone with the snow.

questions.prompt: Why are the fairies “not afraid”? What do they do?
facilitatorNotes: They do not understand death; they notice only the “glittering things,” a ring and a chain. They kneel and play with them, and take them home to play with tomorrow. “Eerily” tells the reader to shiver even though the fairies do not.
evidence: And eerily played
And were not afraid.

questions.prompt: The speaker asks “you” a question, then tells about himself. How was his first meeting with death like the fairies’, and how was it different?
facilitatorNotes: Like them, he came on it “flower-guided,” in the middle of play, without expecting it. Unlike them, he understood it at once, with sorrow and dread, and he still hates taking anything from the dead (“hated and hate”). Some readers think the fairies cannot be blamed, since they do not know; others share his feeling that the ring and chain should have been left alone.
evidence: Did you not come flower-guided
And I hated and hate

readings.title: Now Close the Windows
readings.challenge: Notice what the speaker wants to see but not hear, and think about why a poem near the end of a book might ask for quiet.
readings.focus: With the birds gone and spring far off, the speaker shuts out the sound of the wind and watches the world move in silence.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” Frost’s note in the contents: “It is time to make an end of speaking.” This poem comes near the end of the book. Ere means before; to resume is to begin again; marshes are wet lands, loud with frogs and birds in spring.

excerpt.locator: “Now Close the Windows,” complete poem; opens “Now close the windows and hush all the fields; If the trees must, let them silently toss;…”; closes “…the earliest bird: So close the windows and not hear the wind, But see all wind-stirred.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker want shut out, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Sound: the fields hushed, the trees tossing silently. The singing season is over, and it will be “long” before the marshes and the earliest bird begin again.
evidence: Now close the windows and hush all the fields;
If the trees must, let them silently toss;

questions.prompt: “No bird is singing now, and if there is, / Be it my loss.” What does he mean?
facilitatorNotes: Even if one late bird is still singing, he would rather not hear it, and accepts missing it. Perhaps one lonely song would only make the silence sadder; perhaps he is ready for quiet. Readers may hear calm, or something close to giving up.
evidence: No bird is singing now, and if there is,
Be it my loss.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between hearing the wind and seeing “all wind-stirred”?
facilitatorNotes: Through closed windows he can watch everything move, trees tossing and grass bending, without the noise. The world goes on, but at a distance, like a film with the sound off. Some readers find that peaceful; others find it lonely.
evidence: So close the windows and not hear the wind,
But see all wind-stirred.

questions.prompt: Frost’s note says “It is time to make an end of speaking.” What else, besides a season, might be ending?
facilitatorNotes: The book is nearly over, so the poet is closing his own song; it may also be the end of a time in his life. “It will be long ere” promises that new songs will come, though not soon. Readers may prefer to read it simply as late autumn, and the poem supports that too.
evidence: It will be long ere the marshes resume,
It will be long ere the earliest bird:

readings.title: My Butterfly
readings.challenge: Untangle old-fashioned words and long sentences to follow a young man’s grief for a butterfly, and for more than a butterfly.
readings.focus: Finding a butterfly’s broken wing in autumn, the speaker remembers its summer flight and one dizzy day when the wind flung its wing against his cheek.
readings.context: A Boy’s Will (1913) was Robert Frost’s first book of poems, published in London when he was thirty-nine; this is the 1915 New York printing. Its title comes from a line by Longfellow, “A boy’s will is the wind’s will.” “My Butterfly” was the first poem Frost ever sold, to a New York magazine in 1894, when he was twenty. His note in the contents: “There are things that can never be the same.” Thine, thee, thou and thy are old forms of your and you; emulous means competing, here the flowers that rivalled the butterfly’s colours; daft means foolish; frighted means frightened; oft means often; dappled means spotted; dalliance is playful idling; precipitate means headlong; “I wist” means I knew; rife means everywhere; languor is lazy dreaminess; distraught means upset; a zephyr is a light breeze; the eaves are the overhanging edge of a roof.

excerpt.locator: “My Butterfly,” complete poem; opens “Thine emulous fond flowers are dead, too, And the daft sun-assaulter, he That frighted…”; closes “…I said, And the strange birds say. I found it with the withered leaves Under the eaves.”.

questions.prompt: Whom is the speaker talking to, and what has happened to it?
facilitatorNotes: A butterfly, now dead. Its flowers are dead too, and the foolish creature that used to frighten it is “fled or dead”; only the speaker is left to mourn. At the end he finds its broken wing among the withered leaves.
evidence: Save only me
I found that wing broken to-day!

questions.prompt: How long ago does the summer seem, and how did the butterfly fly then?
facilitatorNotes: Snow has not fallen yet, but summer seems “forever” ago. Then the butterfly flew with “all the dazzling other ones,” tossed, tangled and whirled “Like a limp rose-wreath in a fairy dance.”
evidence: But it is long ago—
Tossed, tangled, whirled and whirled above,

questions.prompt: The speaker gives two explanations for the butterfly’s death. What are they?
facilitatorNotes: Fate made it “for the pleasure of the wind,” to be tossed about and worn out; or God let it flutter free, then, afraid it would go too far, snatched it back too roughly. Both make a fragile, careless creature the plaything of something stronger. Some readers find the picture of God grabbing too hard strange; others find it moving.
evidence: That fate had made thee for the pleasure of the wind,
Snatched thee, o'er eager, with ungentle grasp.

questions.prompt: Why does he remember the day the wing touched his cheek? What might Frost’s note, “There are things that can never be the same,” mean here?
facilitatorNotes: On a dreamy, dizzy summer day, when he was too upset to speak, the breeze threw the butterfly’s wing against his face: a wild, sudden touch of beauty. Now that same wing lies broken. The summer, the butterfly, perhaps his own young happiness are gone for good. Many readers think he mourns more than a butterfly; ask what else it might be.
evidence: But the wild touch of thy dye-dusty wing!
I found it with the withered leaves
